title: Interfaces
summary: Describe what a type can do without saying how, so code can work with anything that fits.

steps.title: A contract, not a class
body: A checkout needs to take a payment. It should not care whether that is a card, a gift card or something invented next year. It only cares that the thing **can pay**.
An **interface** writes that down. It lists members a type must have, with no code inside them.
A class **implements** the interface by naming it after a colon and supplying every member as `public`:
- Interface names start with `I` by convention.
- Members of an interface are public automatically, so you write no modifier there.
- Miss a member out and the class does not compile. The contract is enforced.

options: A variable of type `IPaymentMethod` can hold any object whose class implements it
`new IPaymentMethod()` creates an empty payment method
It stores the payment amount in a field
Only one class in a program may implement it
steps.explain: An interface has no code and no data of its own, so there is nothing to `new`. It is a type you can use for variables and parameters, and any number of classes can implement it.

steps.prompt: Define a notifier contract and one class that fulfils it.
steps.explain: C# uses the same colon for implementing an interface as for inheriting. The implementing method must be `public`, and it does not use `override`.

steps.title: Program to the interface
body: The payoff comes when a method asks for the **interface** instead of a particular class.
`NotifyShipped` knows nothing about email or SMS. It depends only on the contract. That is called **decoupling**, and it buys you three things:
- Add a `PushNotifier` later and `NotifyShipped` does not change by one character.
- Swap the real thing for a fake in a test: a notifier that just remembers what it was asked to send.
- The method's signature tells the truth about what it needs.

steps.prompt: One array, two implementations. What does this print?
code: INotifier[] notifiers = { new EmailNotifier(), new SmsNotifier() };
steps.explain: The loop only knows `INotifier`. Each object runs its own `Send`.

steps.title: Two kinds of discount
prompt: Write an interface and two classes that implement it.
- `decimal Apply(decimal price)`: returns the price after the discount
- takes a fixed amount off, but never goes below `0`
template: Dojo.Check("IDiscount is an interface", typeof(IDiscount).IsInterface, "Declare it with the interface keyword");
foreach (IDiscount dojoD in new IDiscount[] { dojoTen, dojoFifteen }) dojoPrice = dojoD.Apply(dojoPrice);
Dojo.Eq("both discounts in a row through IDiscount: 100 -> 90 -> 75", 75m, dojoPrice);
hints: The interface member has no body and no `public`: `decimal Apply(decimal price);`
Each class needs `: IDiscount` on its first line, a private field to remember the constructor argument, and a `public decimal Apply(decimal price)` method.
For `AmountOff`: if the amount is bigger than the price, return `0m`; otherwise return `price - _amount`.

steps.title: More than one interface
body: A class can have only one base class, but it can implement **as many interfaces as it likes**. Each one is a separate ability.
A method that only prints asks for an `IPrintable`. It never finds out the object can also export. Small interfaces keep each piece of code knowing as little as it needs.
If there is a base class too, it goes first: `class Invoice : Document, IPrintable, IExportable`.

items: A class can use several at once
Lists what a type can do, with no data
Can store data in instance fields
Can declare a member that others must supply

steps.title: Interface or abstract class?
body: Both leave members for someone else to fill in. Choose by asking what the types actually share.
| Shared code and fields | yes | no |
| How many per class | one | many |
- `SalariedEmployee` and `HourlyEmployee` share a name and a `ToString`. They **are** employees. A base class holds the shared part.
- An email sender and an SMS gateway share **no code at all**. They simply both **can** send. That is an interface.
When unsure, start with an interface. It asks the least of the classes that use it, and you can always add a base class later to share code between some of them.

steps.prompt: A report needs to be saved to a file, a database, or cloud storage. The three savers share no code, and a test should be able to use a fake one. What fits best?
options: An abstract class `ReportStore` with fields for the file path and the database connection
A static class `ReportSaver` with three methods
One class with a `string kind` parameter and a big `switch`
steps.explain: Nothing is shared except the ability to save, so a contract is all you need. The static class and the big `switch` both have to be edited for every new kind of storage, and neither can be swapped for a fake.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so every notifier in the list sends `Paid`.
steps.explain: The list is typed by the interface, so it can hold any mix of notifiers, and the loop never needs to know which is which.

steps.title: A checkout that takes anything
prompt: Build a small payment system. The tests will also pass in a payment method **you have never seen**, so `Checkout` must depend only on the interface.
- `Pay` returns `true` when the amount is within the limit
- `Balance`: readable by anyone, settable only inside the class
- `Pay` takes the amount off the balance and returns `true`, or changes nothing and returns `false` when the balance is too low
- `static string Pay(IPaymentMethod method, decimal amount)` returns `"Paid 30 by Card"` when the payment works and `"Card declined"` when it does not, using the method's own `Name`
starter: public static string Pay(IPaymentMethod method, decimal amount)
solution: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
public static string Pay(IPaymentMethod method, decimal amount)
template: Dojo.Eq("a card with limit 100 pays 100", true, dojoCard.Pay(100m));
Dojo.Eq("a card with limit 100 refuses 100.01", false, dojoCard.Pay(100.01m));
Dojo.Eq("GiftCard.Name is Gift card", "Gift card", dojoGiftAsPayment.Name);
Dojo.Eq("a 50 gift card pays 20", true, dojoGiftAsPayment.Pay(20m));
Dojo.Eq("Refund(5) through IRefundable raises Balance to 35", 35m, dojoGift.Balance);

Dojo.Check("GiftCard.Balance cannot be set from outside", typeof(GiftCard).GetProperty("Balance") is { } dojoBal && dojoBal.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "Use: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }");
Dojo.Eq("Checkout.Pay(giftCard, 1) once it is empty", "Gift card declined", Checkout.Pay(dojoGift, 1m));
Dojo.Eq("Checkout works with a payment method it has never seen (accepts)", "Paid 12 by Voucher", Checkout.Pay(new DojoVoucher(true), 12m));
Dojo.Eq("Checkout works with a payment method it has never seen (declines)", "Voucher declined", Checkout.Pay(new DojoVoucher(false), 12m));
hints: `IRefundable` has one line inside: `void Refund(decimal amount);`. `GiftCard` lists both interfaces after the colon, separated by a comma.
`Name` can be a computed property: `public string Name => "Card";`

`Checkout.Pay` calls `method.Pay(amount)` and builds the text from `method.Name`: `$"Paid {amount} by {method.Name}"` or `$"{method.Name} declined"`. Never mention `CardPayment` or `GiftCard` inside it.
